resources.string: Sleevesight

Sleevesight reads what your music player is playing, looks it up in the sources you switch on, and has the AI service you choose write about it. Before you start, here is what it reads, and what leaves your phone.
What it reads

Sleevesight needs notification access, which is how Android lets an app read what a player is playing: the title, artists, album, length and cover. It ignores the notifications themselves, and it never touches the audio.
What leaves the phone, and to whom

To the sources you switch on, such as MusicBrainz and Wikipedia: the title and artists, cleaned of tags such as “2006 Remaster”, and the album name. This is for the playing track and, while “Prepare the next track” is on, for the next one in the player’s queue.

To the AI service you choose: the title, artists and album, what the sources found, and your style setting, including any text you write there. This is for the playing track and, by default, for the next one in the queue.
To Spotify, only if you connect a Spotify account: requests for the playlist or album being played, made with your own token.
To the player’s image server, when a player gives the cover only as a web address: a request for that image.
Each of these services also sees your phone’s IP address, as every service you connect to does.
What stays on the phone

Nothing else leaves the phone. The length and cover of each track, the list of tracks played, and the record of track changes used to tell your skips from natural ends stay on it, and are left out of Android’s backup. Your API keys are stored encrypted and never logged.
No accounts of our own, no telemetry, no crash reporting, no analytics, no ads.
